title: F2 – Strategic decision-making biases
source: Zusammenfassung von Session 2 „Strategic decision-making biases“ sowie Kahneman, Lovallo & Sibony (2011), Luca (2021), Sunstein & Hastie (2014) und Powell, Lovallo & Fox (2011)

blocks.text: Every decision-maker faces biases. The session moves in three steps: information perception → information filtering → strategic decision-making.

Bounded rationality (Herbert Simon): decision-makers do not maximize; they choose the first satisfactory alternative (“satisficing”) without evaluating all options, using heuristics – mental shortcuts that usually work but are not always accurate.
Two thinking systems (Kahneman): System 1 = fast, intuitive, associative; System 2 = slow, deliberate, logical. They operate in parallel – and both can be correct or biased.
Good strategy starts with causal thinking: correlation does not imply causation.
Knowing about biases does not remove them. The remedy is the process: independent review, checklists, premortems, red teams and choice architecture (Kahneman et al.; Powell et al.).
We interpret ambiguous cues; the meaning is shaped by experience, knowledge, expectations and identity – not only by the cue. Perceptual illusions can lead to false conclusions.
Inattentional blindness: when focused on a demanding task, we fail to notice unexpected events in full view (gorilla video, unicycling clown). Causes:
children: Cognitive load: too much information, multitasking, tiredness
Expectations: expecting one event blocks attention to others (magic tricks)
Attentional capacities: personal (expertise) and situational (tiredness, drugs) factors

blocks.text: Scarcity vs abundance: with too much information we filter pieces out; with too little we fill the gaps with meaning.
Categorization: sorting objects into categories with a “prototype” lets us respond quickly – but it also biases (“imagine a CEO”: man or woman?).
Conjunction fallacy (Linda problem, Tversky & Kahneman): people judge “bank teller AND feminist” as more likely than “bank teller”, although P(A and B) ≤ P(A). Cause: representativeness heuristic.

Out-group homogeneity bias: “they are alike; we are diverse.” In-group favoritism: we favour members of our own group, even when groups are assigned randomly – explained by social identity theory (Tajfel): self-esteem comes from the groups we belong to.

Dichotomous thinking (Oshio 2009): preference for dichotomy, dichotomous belief, profit-and-loss thinking. Low tolerance of ambiguity (Bochner 1965): need for categorization and certainty, premature closure, rejection of the unusual.
Strategic relevance: a diagnosis is an act of categorization and a decision is a binary go/no-go – but strategic problems are ambiguous. Check at each step whether two problems are really similar.
Experts have richer schemas but risk cognitive entrenchment (Dane 2010) – the Einstellung effect: prioritizing the known solution over new, more appropriate ones.

Confirmation bias: searching for, attending to and believing information that fits prior beliefs. Mechanisms: selective exposure, selective perception, selective retention. Amplified by the “filter bubble” (Pariser 2011).
Ice cream and sunburn co-occur; baths and lower heart disease co-occur – the data are fine, the causal interpretation is the problem (Luca 2021).
Four sources of endogeneity (inability to claim causality):
children: Simultaneity / reverse causation: does A cause B or B cause A? (police budgets and crime)
Omitted variable: a confounder C drives both A and B → spurious correlation (stress and leisure time behind baths and heart health)
Measurement error: A or B is badly measured (how to measure money, happiness?)
Selection bias: the sample is not random – sampling, survivorship, attrition, non-response, volunteer and undercoverage bias

blocks.text: Survivorship bias (Abraham Wald, WWII bombers): studying only planes that came back suggested reinforcing the damaged areas – but the planes hit elsewhere never returned. Learning from success stories only cannot reveal what causes success.

Remedies: theory and common sense, temporal antecedence, controlled or natural experiments, instrumental variables; ask how the data were generated (eBay ads: the spend mostly reached people who would have bought anyway).

sections.heading: Before you make that big decision (Kahneman, Lovallo & Sibony 2011)

blocks.text: We cannot catch our own System 1 errors, but we can review other people's recommendations. A 12-question checklist:
children: Self-interest, affect heuristic (in love with the proposal), groupthink (was dissent explored?)
Saliency (one memorable analogy), confirmation (real alternatives?), availability (what is missing?)
Anchoring (where do the numbers come from?), halo effect, sunk costs and endowment
Over-optimism / planning fallacy / competitor neglect, disaster neglect (premortem), loss aversion

blocks.text: Works only for important, recurring decisions and if the reviewer is independent of the team.

Sunstein & Hastie (2014): groups often amplify errors through informational signals and reputational pressure. Failure modes: amplified errors, cascades, polarization, common-knowledge effect (hidden profiles).
Correctives: silence the leader, prime critical thinking, reward group success, assign roles, devil's advocate (weak), red teams, Delphi method / anonymous voting.

Powell, Lovallo & Fox (2011): behavioral strategy brings realistic psychology into strategic management – a fourth pillar next to market power, resources and innovation. Individual debiasing largely fails; the firm's choice architecture matters.
Choosing the first satisfactory option instead of the optimal one (Simon).
Simple judgmental strategies – mental shortcuts between automatic perception and deliberate reasoning.
Failing to see unexpected events while attention is focused elsewhere.
Experts prioritize the familiar solution over new, more appropriate ones (cognitive entrenchment).
Looking for, noticing and remembering information that fits prior beliefs.
Only surviving (successful) cases are observed, so the causes of success are misread.
A third variable affects both A and B and creates a spurious correlation.

sections.heading: Further thinking: using F2 in the exam

blocks.text: When a case shows a founder or CEO deciding on a bold move, name the concrete bias (overconfidence, confirmation, sunk cost, halo, survivorship) and a process remedy (premortem, red team, outside view, reference class).
When a case cites a correlation (“customers who use feature X stay longer”), discuss reverse causality, a confounder and selection – then propose an experiment.
